items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: There are true statements about numbers that cannot be proved
items.claim: Hilbert (1900) hoped to put mathematics on a complete, consistent axiomatic foundation. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved it impossible. Any system of axioms expressive enough to do basic arithmetic contains true statements that the system cannot prove.
items.prompt: What's the heart of Gödel's argument?

options.text: Gödel constructed a self-referential statement G: 'G cannot be proved within this system'. If the system could prove G, the system would prove something false (contradiction). If the system can't prove G, then G is true and unprovable

items.reveal:
Gödel encoded statements about mathematics AS numbers (Gödel numbering), so the system could 'talk about itself'. He then constructed a sentence asserting its own unprovability.

First incompleteness theorem: any consistent system strong enough to express arithmetic contains a true statement it cannot prove.
Second incompleteness theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency from within itself.

The results devastated Hilbert's program. They also bounded what computers can do: the halting problem (Turing 1936) is undecidable in essentially the same way.

Gödel was 25 when he proved it. Hilbert took it badly. Gödel later starved himself to death (1978) — convinced his food was being poisoned, he stopped eating when his wife was hospitalised.

Mathematics is still consistent (presumably), still useful, still extending — just provably incomplete.
items.why: Mathematics is treated as a closed, fully derivable system. Gödel showed any rich enough system has fundamental gaps — true things it can never prove.
